extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, epistemology, and the foundations of mathematics and science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for what counts as scientific knowledge and valid mathematical exposition: the relation of perception and demonstration, the role of judgment, appropriate methods for mathematics versus natural science, and the use of induction and experiment. Targets philosophers, mathematicians, and teachers deciding how to justify and present truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific character: systematic form (general-to-particular)
rubrics_metrics.description: The special characteristic of science does not lie in certainty but in the systematic form of knowledge, based on the gradual descent from the general to the particular (satisfying the law of homogeneity and that of specification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science should organize knowledge by subordinating concept-spheres according to determinations so that knowledge descends by degrees from general concepts through intermediate concepts to particulars. The aim is facilitating rational knowledge by its form and permitting the completeness of rational knowledge, not merely securing greater certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary source of truth: perception (a priori and a posteriori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception, partly a priori and partly empirical a posteriori, is the source of all truth and the foundation of all science; primary judgments are created directly out of perception and are to science what the sun is to the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give priority to judgments founded directly on perception. Logic is exceptional (as direct knowledge of its own laws), but generally truths ultimately rest on perception; demonstrations must ultimately be grounded in undemonstrated perceptual truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for immediate evidence over demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: A directly established truth is as much to be preferred to a truth established by demonstration as water from the spring is to water from the aqueduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct perception (or a priori intuition) is available, rely on it rather than constructing lengthy syllogistic demonstrations. Demonstrations are useful chiefly when immediate evidence is remote or contested; they are tools for disputation rather than the primary source of insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty of judgment: form concepts accurately from perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty of judgment consists in the power of rightly and accurately carrying over into abstract consciousness what is known in perception, mediating between understanding and reason; deficiency in judgment is silliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good judgment must both abstract commonality into one concept and discern differences into separate concepts, avoiding failure to grasp partial differences or identities. Only exceptional individual judgment advances science, but healthy reason can still perform demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of syllogistic demonstration and danger of sophisms
rubrics_metrics.description: All demonstration is syllogistic; syllogisms are perfectly certain in form but very uncertain in matter because concepts are often vague and intersecting, creating room for paralogisms and sophisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat syllogistic proofs with caution: they expose conclusions to error when the choice of major or middle terms is ambiguous. Use demonstrations only when immediate perception is unavailable; beware of sophistical proofs that exploit vague concept-spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical method should preserve a priori intuition (avoid throwing away perceptual evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics often deliberately throws away the evidence of perception peculiar to it and substitutes logical demonstration; this is a perversion—Euclid's method is like cutting off legs to go on crutches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting mathematical truths, retain and appeal to the special a priori intuitions of space and time. Avoid replacing perceptual insight with purely conceptual demonstrations that obscure the inner connection of geometric facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical exposition must show the 'why' not only the 'that'
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematics we should combine the knowledge that a thing is as it is with the knowledge why it is so; Euclid's demonstrations often tell us only that something is true, not why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor proofs and expositions that reveal the ground of being (the inner connection and necessity) rather than only providing logical grounds of knowledge. Anti-patterns: proofs that feel like juggling tricks, use arbitrary constructions without showing their rationale, or leave learners with rote results but no insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer analytical method in mathematical teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: An analysis of the process of thought in the first discovery of a geometrical truth (the analytical method) is preferable to Euclid's synthetic method for imparting real insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure instruction to retrace discovery and exhibit why relations follow from intuition (a priori perception). The analytical method may be harder for complicated truths but yields deeper understanding; curricular reformers have attempted this approach (example: Kosack).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms and geometric truths are immediate metaphysical truths (a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical propositions are metaphysical truths and are, like axioms, immediately evident and known a priori; none of these forms is superior to the others in their immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to derive the necessity of space-relations from pure logical principles (principle of contradiction); treat geometric truths as immediate intuitions whose necessity is on par with logical axioms. Anti-pattern: reducing geometric necessity to mere formal logical demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic rests on pure perception in time (counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic and algebra permit direct evidence through pure perception in time (counting); arithmetic is essentially a method of abbreviating counting and treats each counted instance as an axiom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept counting as immediate a priori intuition for arithmetic truths; the introduction of formal logical proofs into arithmetic is unnecessary because counting itself provides evidence. Recognize limitations of intuitive counting for large numbers where abstraction and numeral systems assist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural sciences rely on induction and experiment; certainty is approximate
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science (physics, astronomy, physiology) rests upon induction—comparing many perceptions—and on hypotheses later confirmed by experience; only purposeful experiments let knowledge proceed from cause to effect and thereby increase certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction from many observed cases and designed experiments to approach certainty; accept that hypotheses may be false and must be revised. Treat repeated empirical confirmation as practical near-certainty while acknowledging the residual possibility of error (e.g., counterfeit cases that deceive senses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of sufficient reason as basis of all explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: All explanation consists of reduction to the principle of sufficient reason; this principle expresses the universal form of all our ideas and knowledge and is itself neither susceptible of explanation nor in need of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame explanations as reductions to reasons that make consequents necessary; recognize that the principle of sufficient reason underlies different forms of explanation (ground of being, change, action, knowing) and is the ultimate presupposition of explanatory discourse.
